title:
Liliata rutilantium.
 Turma circumdet.
 Iubilantium te virginum
html_source:
Liliata rutilantium te confessorum turma circumdet: iubilantium te virginum chorus excipiat, translates as:

May the troop of confessors, glowing like lilies, surround you. May the choir of virgins, jubilant, take you in.

The source of these words is in the Prayers for the Dying in the Catholic Layman’s Missal.

The Missal contains instructions on the acceptable use of the prayer: “In the absence of a priest, these prayers for commending a dying person to God, may be read by any responsible person, man or woman.” The prayer was chanted, then, by one or more of the family members who “prayed on their knees” while gathered around the bedside of Stephen’s dying mother, as Stephen recalls in Telemachus the first time he thinks of the Latin lines. Stephen continues to recall snatches of the two sentences during the rest of his day: once more in Telemachus, once in Aeolus, once in Circe, and once in Ithaca.

Joyce Project
